Full breakdown at austinkocher.substack.com 
TRAC's February 2026 court operations update: tracreports.org/whatsnew/ema…
TRAC quick facts (updated regularly): tracreports.org/immigration/…
Immigration Policy Tracking Project on judge firings: immpolicytracking.org/polici…

The numbers alone can’t answer the central question: Is the decline in asylum grants about changing applicant profiles, or pressure on immigration judges? The implications for due process are enormous.

Immigration judges completed 81,932 cases in March 2026 alone. Of those, 57,874 ended in removal orders and another 9,075 in voluntary departure orders. This is part of an FY2026 trend where 80% of completed cases end in deportation.
In February 2026, just 33.3% of immigrants had legal representation when removal orders were issued. Most people facing deportation are going through high-stakes legal proceedings without a lawyer.

A 2026 investigation by NYT reported that the immigration judges fired since January 2025 disproportionately had three things in common: Democratic appointments, experience representing immigrants, and above-average asylum grant rates.

After peaking at 3.4 million cases in December 2025, the immigration court backlog has declined modestly. Courts are completing cases at 1.65 times the pace of new filings, even after more than 100 immigration judges were fired since January 2025.
So far in FY2026, immigration courts granted asylum in under 10% of cases, the lowest rate ever recorded. Meanwhile, the same court system is carrying a backlog of 3.3 million pending cases.

More on my Substack. austinkocher.substack.com 

JAMA study (April 16, 2026): jamanetwork.com/journals/jam…

CNN investigation on understaffing and deaths (May 15, 2026): cnn.com/2026/05/15/us/ice-im…

My detention data analysis: austinkocher.substack.com/p/…
A key limitation: ICE has not released all required death reports, and cause of death is still undetermined in many recent cases The actual toll is likely higher than what's officially documented.

This happened as key detention oversight bodies (CRCL, the USCIS Ombudsman, and the Immigration Detention Ombudsman) were gutted or shuttered, and then only partially reopened with contractor staffing.

JAMA’s authors frame this as “longstanding failures” intensified by policies that expanded detention capacity, weakened oversight, and worsened conditions. An assessment from the authors thats worth noting.
CNN reported on May 15 that ICE detention surged past 70,000, higher than under any prior administration, while medical staffing at some facilities failed to rise proportionally.

From FY2004 to Jan. 19, 2026, the study documented at least 272 ICE custody deaths. Since then, deaths have continued to rise, with 47+ people dying in ICE custody since Trump took office in Jan. 2025.

A peer-reviewed JAMA study published Apr. 16, 2026 found ICE detention deaths in partial FY2026 reached 88.9 per 100,000; a 22-year high with nearly 7x FY2023’s 13.0 rate, and higher than the COVID-era spike.

David Hausman and the Deportation Data Project are doing essential public work. 

Deportation Data Project (April 7, 2026): deportationdata.org/analysis…

ICE data through March 2026 (open access): deportationdata.org/data/ice…

My Substack: austinkocher.substack.com

A small dip in enforcement followed the Minneapolis killings of Renée Good and Alex Pretti in January 2026. The DDP data shows it was real but modest, it didn't fundamentally change the trajectory of ICE street arrests, raids, and other aggressive enforcement tactics.

What stands out is that voluntary departures and returns increased 28-fold. That means large numbers of people chose to leave rather than fight their cases, partly bc they don’t want to spend months sitting in detention.

ICE increased detention beds for interior arrests 4.5x. Release within 60 days of arrest (under Biden ppl w/out crim. records = 35%), dropped to 7% under Trump. Lower release rates drive numbers up, which means ICE isn’t just arresting more ppl, it’s holding them longer.

The pattern that gets less attention than the raw totals are the arrests of people with no criminal convictions, which has increased more than eightfold. The primary mechanism is aggressive enforcement of people with no convictions.
The report, by David Hausman (UC Berkeley) and Graeme Blair (UCLA), covers ICE data through March 10, 2026. It's the most comprehensive independent analysis of first-year enforcement to date.
